rationale: B wins because it treats the $400M number like a reporting problem, not a trophy: "top creators collectively" is a self-selected numerator with an undisclosed denominator. A has useful bones, but "$400 million in creator earnings is an inconvenient number for the subscription fatigue narrative" imports a whole discourse the update did not prove. B is less padded, tougher on proof, and much less likely to send a founder into a reporter's inbox carrying a glass jaw.
gaps_in_A: "subscription fatigue narrative" / "widely published since 2022–2023" is not in the update. That may be true in the world, but this exercise gave no evidence for it, so the contrarian angle is doing borrowed-gravitas cosplay.

"implying $40M or more flowed to Substack from top creators alone" assumes the $400M figure is subscription revenue subject to the 10% cut and that the accounting basis is clear. A later asks for clarity, but the headline argument already spent the money.
"The broader debate over creator monetization models is active" is a soft news peg. If you cannot name the live debate from supplied facts, do not smuggle it in as urgency.

Five angles is one too many here. The YouTube economics angle and the creator-operator angle both lean on the same unresolved proof: whether creators actually want Substack video instead of using existing video platforms.
gaps_in_B: "Substack has stopped competing with Mailchimp and started competing with YouTube" is punchy but imports Mailchimp as the old competitive set. The update says newsletter platform, not email-marketing competitor.

"the feed that rewards something they didn't sign up to make" overstates the labor angle. The update says TikTok-style feed, not that video gets boosted or text gets punished; B does ask the right proof question later, but the line is ahead of the evidence.

"Video hosting is one of the most expensive infrastructure commitments a platform can make" is plausible business context, not supplied grounding. Fine as a question, dangerous as a premise unless sourced.

"won't say how the split works" is a little prosecutorial. The facts say individual creator earnings are not disclosed; the denominator and gross/net questions are fair, but 'won't say' implies a refusal not shown in the update.
